finalResponse:
# Lead-Time Recovery Plan: From 14 Weeks to 6–7, With Every Quality Gate Intact

Three functions — production, quality, and sales — have each been carrying their own pressure, and each sees a different part of this problem. None of them is wrong. The 14 weeks is not anyone's failure; it is the arithmetic sum of three groups each doing exactly what they were asked to do. This plan succeeds by giving all three a shared goal, shared facts, and shared protection — and by treating the warranty experience of two years ago not as a scar, but as the organization's most valuable asset: precise knowledge of what must never be rushed.

## 1. The Business Case

One in three deals lost on delivery speed is the financial engine of this plan. Illustrative figures below — the pod's first task, working quietly with finance and sales colleagues, is to rebuild them with actuals before any spending decision is taken.

| Element | Illustrative Estimate | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Quoted demand lost annually to lead time | ~$16M | $50M annual quoted pipeline × ~33% lost on delivery |
| Revenue recovered if half of those deals are won | ~$8M/yr | Parity on standard configurations + reliable promises on specials |
| Contribution margin recovered | ~$2.4–2.8M/yr | At 30–35% contribution |
| One-time investment | ~$2.0–3.5M | Module stock build ($1.5–2.5M working capital, partially offset by consignment), second-source qualification ($100–300k), operator training ($150–250k), digital traveler implementation ($200–400k), pod backfill (2–3 FTE-equivalents) |
| Recurring cost | ~$300–500k/yr | Carrying cost at 15–20% of module inventory; supplier capacity reservation fees |
| Payback | Under 12 months | Recovering even one deal in six covers the recurring costs several times over |

No executive is asked to approve this on placeholders. The structure is the commitment; the numbers are confirmed together, early, before money moves.

## 2. Where the 14 Weeks Actually Live

Before changing anything, the organization needs one shared fact base. Timestamp the last 20–30 orders end-to-end, separating touch time from queue time. This must be introduced with care: the audit maps the *process*, never the people, and that pledge is made explicitly and kept visibly. Blame thrives in opacity; it is very hard to blame a timestamp.

Expected decomposition, to be confirmed by the audit:

| Bucket | Typical Range | What to Look For |
|---|---|---|
| Order-to-release | 2–3 weeks | Quote clarifications, incomplete specs, engineering review queues |
| Long-lead purchased items | 4–6 weeks | Castings, drives, specialty components — often the true critical path |
| Production queue vs. build | 2–3 weeks | Units waiting days for cells that touch them for hours |
| Certification logistics | 2–3 weeks | Inspector availability, third-party witness scheduling, documentation assembled after the work instead of during it |
| Stacked buffers | 1–2 weeks | Each function quietly padding to protect itself; buffers compound |

In parallel, codify the warranty post-mortem — not to assign fault, which would only reopen old wounds, but to convert it into an explicit **"never again" list**: the specific shortcuts that caused the spike, written down as hard design constraints. This list is what allows Quality to shift from veto-by-delay to veto-by-design, a far more honorable and far less lonely role.

## 3. The Core Strategy — and Its Safety Net

The central question: *why does the certification clock start only when the order arrives?* If the product is even partially modular, the largest lever is **assemble-to-order**: build and fully certify standard modules to stock, in calm conditions, on your own schedule. When an order lands, only final assembly, final test, and final certification remain. The gates do not disappear — they happen before the customer's clock starts.

This lever, however, rests on one load-bearing assumption: that the certification regime permits it. The plan therefore gates the inventory spend on that answer, and carries a contingency for every outcome:

- **Path A — Full pre-certification permitted.** Proceed as designed; standard configurations reach 6–7 weeks.
- **Path B — Partial permission.** Witnessed batch inspection, periodic surveillance of stocked modules, or internal inspectors qualified as authorized witnesses. Most of the benefit survives; standards land at 7–8 weeks.
- **Path C — Not permitted.** The structural lever is shelved and revisited annually. The remaining levers — queue compression, supplier lead-time reduction, certification logistics, scheduling discipline — still deliver a realistic 8–9 weeks. The roadmap bends; it does not collapse.

The certification body is approached in weeks 2–6, early and respectfully, with a quality plan in hand rather than a request for concession. That relationship is an investment regardless of the answer. **Decision gate at week 8–10: no module inventory is built until the path is confirmed.** All Phase 1 quick wins proceed in parallel regardless — they are valuable under every path.

## 4. The Workstreams

**Process and flow.** Reduce batch sizes and changeover times in the constrained cells — queue time is batch-size-driven. Run engineering clarification and procurement kickoff concurrently with final design, not after it. Move spec verification to the quote stage, so incomplete orders are caught before they enter the system rather than discovered inside it.

**Inventory and suppliers.** Consignment or vendor-managed stock of the five to ten true long-lead items; framework agreements reserving supplier capacity; rolling forecasts shared with those suppliers — their lead time is partly your forecast silence. Pre-qualify second sources for the longest items, accepting a small volume premium as insurance.

**Scheduling.** Finite-capacity scheduling, or at minimum drum-buffer-rope around the constraint. A reserved fast lane for standard configurations; specials route around it. Quotes generated from the actual schedule, not from habit.

**Quality gates — accelerated, never thinned.** Inspection moves upstream: source inspection, first-article verification, operator in-process checks with proper gauging, so defects are caught where they are created — rework loops are lead time too. Documentation is generated as work happens. Certification witness slots are pre-booked on a rolling forecast, with standing windows negotiated with the third-party body. Every gate that exists today exists at the end; not one is removed, and the "never again" list is enforced by design.

**Configuration control for certified stock.** This is the quiet risk that must be managed from day one: an engineering change to a stocked, certified module can invalidate its certification. Rules: all certified stock serialized and traceable to design revision; any engineering change affecting a certified module requires joint Quality and certification review before release; affected stock is quarantined pending disposition (re-inspect, rework, or scrap); stocked modules sit under a design freeze with planned revision windows, safety-related changes excepted and handled by immediate effectivity with a stock purge protocol; certification validity of stock audited on a fixed cadence.

**Capacity and the transition.** Building modules to stock while working the current backlog must not starve committed orders — that would trade one reputation problem for another. Phase 0 includes a capacity study of the constraint cell against backlog plus the module build plan. The transition is absorbed by: a defined overtime or weekend window on the constraint (temporary, 3–6 months), subcontracting non-certified fabrication and machining to approved suppliers under source inspection, and gradual module coverage — four to six weeks of pilot-family coverage first, not full finished goods. The standing rule: module builds fill slack and added capacity only, never displacing a committed customer order.

**Commercial.** A tiered quoting architecture, validated against a demand Pareto in Phase 0:

| Quote Tier | Target Share | Target Lead Time (Month 12) |
|---|---|---|
| Standard configurations | 60–70% of quotes | 6–7 weeks |
| Configured variants | 20–25% | 8–9 weeks |
| Engineered specials | 10–15% | Honest 10–12, sold on milestone transparency |

Enterprise-weighted average quoted lead time falls from 14 to roughly 7.5–8 — and on the quotes that decide the win rate, it falls by more than half. A quote configurator ties lead time to configuration. Sales incentives gain modest weight on order cleanliness and forecast accuracy; incomplete orders are a hidden delay factory, and today sales bears no cost for them. Two further points: first, verify early what the competitor's "6 weeks" actually covers — quoted versus shipped, and whether it excludes specials; if the real bar is 8, then 7 wins, and the entire problem resizes. Second, matching 6 rather than beating it is sufficient if the promise is *kept* — reliability of the quoted date, milestone transparency, and an unimpeachable certification record become the differentiators.

## 5. What Each Lever Contributes

The Phase 1 target of 14 → 10–11 weeks is derived, not asserted:

| Lever | Mechanism | Expected Saving |
|---|---|---|
| Spec verification at quote; clean order entry | Eliminates clarification loops | 0.5–1.0 wk |
| Concurrent engineering/procurement kickoff | Removes sequential idle time | 0.5–1.0 wk |
| Pre-booked witness slots; documentation-during-work (interim: dedicated documentation coordinator) | Removes certification logistics tail | 1.0–1.5 wks |
| Batch-size reduction and changeover work on constraint | Shrinks queue time | 0.5–1.0 wk |
| Framework agreements on top long-lead items | Shortens true critical path on affected orders | 0.5–1.5 wks |

Savings are not fully additive — the critical path shifts as each lever lands — so the plan commits conservatively to 10–11. Digital travelers are deliberately *not*
